summary: The first live bench of myidsan's session administration, driven across TWO REAL PROCESSES (myidsan plus a relying myseliasan, the whole authorization-code flow, a real non-administrator account), found two real shipped defects. First, sessions issued by the SERVER-RENDERED login page at /api/auth/login were never indexed - and that page is where every relying app's SSO redirect lands, so it is how nearly everybody actually signs in. The bench signed a user in end to end and then found both the user's own session list and the administrator's listing for that account EMPTY while the user was demonstrably signed in at the relying app; revoking answered {"ok":true,"revoked":0} - success, having done nothing. The social-login callback (setOAuthSession, Google/GitHub) had the same gap, so an account that signed in with Google could not be signed out by an administrator at all. Only the JSON local login indexed what it issued. Fixed by pre-minting the session id and indexing on all three paths through one shared helper (apps/myidsan/apis/session_index.go) rather than a third copy. Second, and larger: revoking a session at the identity server did not end it AT THE RELYING APP. myidsan and a relying app are separate processes with separate caches; the relying app is handed myidsan's session id and then mints its own token under its own key, cached under its own TTL - three days by default. The bench watched an administrator revoke an account's sessions, saw the session go 401 at myidsan, and watched the same browser cookie keep working at the fleet console with full access. /api/sso/introspect exists for exactly this and is called by nothing - and could not have been used anyway, since it validates a TOKEN with myidsan's key and the relying app holds its own. Fixed with POST /api/auth/session-status, keyed on the SESSION ID both sides already share and authenticated with the client_id/client_secret pair the relying app already used to redeem its authorization code, so it needs no new configuration on either side; plus a RevocationChecker in the shared auth middleware that re-asks on a TTL and, on a definite negative, deletes the local session entry so every later request is refused with no further round trips. myseliasan wires it using the same CA-trusting HTTP client as the token exchange. The interval is sso.policyCacheTtlSeconds (30s), a config knob that already existed and until now drove nothing at all. The bench scores 27/27 against the fix and 18/27 against unfixed main on one identical set of checks, and MEASURES the propagation window rather than asserting an instant that was never promised: 30.7s against a 30s configured interval.
compatibility: Backward-compatible; no migration needed. The session_index change only starts writing rows that should always have been written - the user_session table and its shape are unchanged, and indexing stays best-effort so a failure can never fail a sign-in that just succeeded. OPERATIONALLY VISIBLE: sessions created through the SSO login page and through social login now APPEAR in /api/session and /api/session-admin where they previously did not, and can now actually be revoked; an operator who had concluded those surfaces were broken will find they now work. Revocation propagation to a relying app is OPT-IN BY CONFIGURATION and switches itself on: myseliasan enables it only when sso.providerBaseUrl, sso.clientId and sso.clientSecret are all set (a standalone install with local accounts only is completely unaffected), and it needs a myidsan new enough to serve /api/auth/session-status - an older one answers 404, which is reported as 'no answer' and fails open, so a mixed-version estate behaves exactly as it does today rather than signing everybody out. DELIBERATE TRADEOFF, stated plainly: the check fails OPEN when the identity server cannot be reached and fails CLOSED only on a definite 'not active'. Failing closed would sign the whole estate out of the fleet console on every myidsan restart or network blip, which is the tool people need most during exactly those incidents; the cost is that an attacker who holds a stolen cookie AND can partition the relying app from the identity server keeps access until the token expires. Unreachability is logged once per interval. Revocation is therefore not instantaneous: it takes effect within sso.policyCacheTtlSeconds (30s by default), measured at 30.7s live. myidsan itself and the appliance apps wire no checker and are bit-for-bit unchanged.
